svg.title: One page of context engineering, drawn by hand
svg.desc: A hand-drawn single-sheet reference for the Context Engineering series, laid out in eight panels. Panel one stacks the six layers of a context window in order — system prompt, tools, memory, retrieved chunks, conversation, and the user instruction, which is placed last, pinned, and never compressed — under a note that a long window is read best at its ends. Panel two gives the four operations, Write, Select, Compress and Isolate, each with its direction, its scope, and its typical move. Panel three lists five ways context fails — distraction, confusion, conflict, lost in the middle, and tool storm — each with its symptom and its first fix. Panel four draws the window as a budget bar with a soft trigger at eighty per cent and a hard one at ninety-five, then the cost facts: output tokens run about five times input, a cache read about a tenth of the input price, a cache write one-and-a-quarter times on the five-minute term and twice on the hour, and the instruction to freeze the prefix so it survives the turn. Panel five runs retrieval end to end in two lanes: offline, ingest to chunk to contextual header to embed to index; online, rewrite to hybrid search to reciprocal-rank-fusion merge to rerank to bookend pack to generation with citations, closing with the four retrieval scores and the test for choosing long context over retrieval. Panel six sets the system prompt as five blocks — identity, rules, format, knowledge, tools — beside the tool catalog iron triangle of catalog size, description quality and selection cost, of which you may pick two. Panel seven stacks the evaluation pyramid from unit tests up through component and end-to-end to online, with the four numbers worth watching and the biases a model judge brings. Panel eight sets four architectural defences against a ship-day checklist. Same eight-panel rhythm as the typeset reference architecture, so the two can be read side by side.
svg.text: Everything the model sees on every call, and the four things you can do about it.
Every call rebuilds all six. The model remembers nothing else.
top-k after hybrid search and rerank
Order is not cosmetic: a long window is read best at its ends.
2 · Four things you can do about it
Every technique in this series is one of these four.
save to a scratchpad, a memory store, or an index
window, summarise, prune, clear tool results
a sub-agent with a window of its own
Most fixes combine two: select less, then compress the rest.
The context was wrong before the model was.
latches on to a stray phrase in the window
first fix — tighten Select; cut the noise
the right fact is there, the wrong one is used
first fix — clearer rules, and an example
two facts in the window contradict each other
first fix — resolve at retrieval; dedupe
a long window, and the middle is ignored
the same useless call, again and again
first fix — trim the catalog; better descriptions
Reach for the first fix before you reach for a bigger model.
4 · The budget, and what it costs
A context window is a budget, not a container.
THE WINDOW · SPENT AND REBUILT EVERY TURN
80 % soft · window, clear tool results, drop priority 3
95 % hard · summarise older turns to a 200-token brief
Output tokens cost about 5x input — keep generations tight.
Cache read is about 10 % of the input price.
Cache write is 1.25x on the 5-minute TTL, 2x on the 1-hour.
Freeze the prefix: stable system prompt and tools first,
volatile user content last, so the cached prefix survives.
Thinking tokens count too — keep traces out of the prefix.
Half of context engineering is deciding what not to put in the window. This is how the rest gets chosen.
OFFLINE · BUILT ONCE, REBUILT WHEN THE CORPUS MOVES
Score the retriever on its own — faithfulness · answer relevancy · context precision · context recall.
Long context or RAG: does the answer need the whole document, is it there at query time, is the cost fine? Any no, retrieve.
one concept each, motivated by a failure
what is available, and when to use it
Catalog size · description quality · selection cost — pick two.
A description is prompt. Name what it does, when to use it,
when not to, the schema, the return shape, the failures.
cost per session · p95 latency · quality · error rate by kind
Judge biases: position, length, self-preference, rubric drift.
Guardrails: validate the schema, retry on invalid, redact.
8 · Four defences, and the list you ship with
1 · The model is not the permission system. Enforce in code.
2 · Constrain the blast radius: least-privileged credentials,
sandboxed tools, a cap on what one run can touch.
3 · Filter at the boundaries: validate args, structure returns.
4 · Never merge untrusted text into trusted context silently.
An AGENTS.md with the five blocks, reviewed like code.
An eval suite that gates the deploy.
A trace on every call, with cost and tokens attached.
A send-gate on every outbound action.
Sub-agent budgets capped, and auto-compaction on.
Context Engineering — a free 30-post series. Prose CC-BY 4.0, code MIT.
